thread.title_full: Weston considers another SAFER referendum after failed levy vote - NewsBreak

author: Shereen Siewert
title: Weston considers another SAFER referendum after failed levy vote - NewsBreak
text:
By Shereen Siewert ,
6 hours ago Weston Municipal Center. Photo courtesy village of Weston. WESTON, Wis. — Weston officials could ask voters again this fall to fund additional fire and EMS staffing, just months after residents rejected a $600,000 public safety levy increase.
The Village Board took no formal action Monday, but trustees discussed whether to pursue another referendum for the South Area Fire and Emergency Response District, known as SAFER, as the district begins planning for its 2027 budget.
The discussion comes about two months after Weston voters rejected an ongoing property tax levy increase that would have helped fund six additional firefighters and paramedics. The referendum failed in April with 58.2% of voters opposed, the same election in which challengers Lisa Beck, Katrina Clark and Brent Olson swept all three open trustee seats.
The issue has remained politically sensitive in Weston, where officials also voted one week after the election to close a 28-year-old tax increment financing district. That closure is expected to release new tax base and add levy capacity, prompting residents to question whether the village had other financial options before asking voters to approve a referendum.
Village Administrator Jami Gebert told trustees that any referendum resolution would need to be adopted and submitted to the Marathon County clerk by Aug. 25 to make the November ballot.
A memo included in the meeting packet from SAFER Fire Chief Finke outlined several staffing scenarios. Keeping staffing at current levels is expected to increase the district’s 2027 budget by about $150,000, largely because of health insurance and other cost increases. Converting part-time positions to full time would add an estimated $210,000. Adding three full-time employees would increase costs by about $450,000, while adding six would raise costs by about $750,000.
Weston pays about 67.5% of SAFER’s costs, while Rib Mountain pays about 32.5%, according to the memo.
Finke wrote that SAFER’s current staffing “does not provide consistent and rapid delivery of fire and EMS services” to the villages it protects. The district’s maximum daily staffing is nine people, with a minimum of seven, but Finke wrote it is “extremely rare” for SAFER to be fully staffed at nine.
The district’s long-term goal, according to the memo, is to reach a minimum of 10 people on duty as often as possible, with 11 as the maximum staffing level. That would allow SAFER to staff three ambulances while maintaining at least minimal fire staffing at each station.
The memo also acknowledged the referendum result.
“My concern is that the voters of the Village had their opportunity to speak with the spring referendum and the majority stated they do not want to spend additional money on fire/EMS funding,” Finke wrote.
During public comment Monday, questions were raised as to why SAFER had more than $1 million in fund balance while officials continue discussing staffing needs and a possible referendum.
SAFER’s May meeting minutes show the district had about $1.287 million in fund balance, though $30,000 was expected to come out because fund balance had been used to offset the current year’s levy. The district’s fund balance policy calls for maintaining 25% to 33% of the budget, and SAFER was at a little more than 32%, according to the minutes.
Gebert said Monday the fund balance is intended for capital needs, not ongoing operations. Using one-time money for staffing would only delay the same budget problem, officials said.
Finke made the same point during the discussion, saying SAFER had already used fund balance to help offset costs and that doing so again would not create a lasting solution.
“It’s not a permanent fix,” Finke said.
The spring referendum would have funded six additional SAFER positions. But trustees discussed whether a smaller staffing increase — potentially three positions — could be more realistic, particularly after the closure of TID #1.
Finance Director Jessica Trautman told the board the village has received an estimate showing the TID closure could add about $503,000 in levy capacity, based partly on estimated growth. But she cautioned that the figure is preliminary and could change by $50,000 to $70,000 once final numbers come in from the state in August.
Trautman also said about $200,000 in wages and benefits currently charged to the TID would come back into the general fund after the district closes. That means the full amount of new levy capacity would not be available for SAFER.
Trustees discussed whether the village could potentially direct about $300,000 more toward SAFER, but no formal proposal was made. Board members also noted that any staffing decision would need to be worked through with Rib Mountain, which shares the district’s costs.
Trustee Lisa Beck said she was concerned that returning to voters in November with another referendum might not produce a different result. She noted that SAFER officials had done public education before the spring election, but voters still rejected the levy increase.
Other trustees said the board needs a clearer picture of the budget before deciding whether to pursue another referendum or identify other funding options. Several also said the village should have a more detailed budget discussion so trustees and residents can better understand where money is going and what tradeoffs are involved.
The SAFER Board is expected to continue discussing staffing in July. Weston’s next regular Village Board meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. Monday, July 20, at the Weston Municipal Center, 4747 Camp Phillips Road.
